topic.title: Standard index form: interpreting, ordering and calculating
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: M7 and M8 are each two 75-minute papers of 50 marks: Paper 1 non-calculator, Paper 2 calculator. Standard form appears in most series and nearly always on Paper 1, in the last third of it — around Q13 to Q17 on M7 and Q4 to Q8 on M8 — and the same item is often printed on both units in the same session. Six shapes recur across the papers read. One mark for a conversion each way, usually as part (a) of a short question (November 2024 M8 P1 Q6, January 2020 M7 P2 Q14). Two marks for a multiplication or a division with the answer demanded in standard form (Summer 2022 M7 P1 Q13 and M8 P1 Q7, November 2021 M7 P1 Q14). Three marks for a chain such as AB divided by C (November 2023 M7 P1 Q14 and M8 P1 Q5, marked A3). Three marks for a percentage change applied to a standard-form quantity (Summer 2025 M7 P1 Q16 and M8 P1 Q7). Three marks for putting three expressions in order with working demanded (November 2025 M7 P1 Q17). Two marks for a unit conversion or a comparison across units (Summer 2024 M7 P1 Q15, Summer 2026 M7 P2 Q17 and M8 P2 Q8), and occasionally three marks for recovering two unknown indices from a printed pair of results (Summer 2023 M7 P1 Q11 and M8 P1 Q4). Schemes run MA1 for the set-up and MA1 or A1 for the answer in the demanded form; the percentage version runs MA1 then A1 then A1, and the ordering version M1 A1 for the values then A1 for the order.
mustMemorise: a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10 and n a whole number, positive or negative
Multiply: multiply the front numbers and add the powers. Divide: divide the front numbers and subtract the powers
Add or subtract: make the powers equal first, then combine the front numbers and keep the shared power
(a × 10ⁿ)^k = a^k × 10^(nk) — the power of ten is multiplied by k, never added to itself
Re-normalise at the end every time: 11.7 × 10⁸ becomes 1.17 × 10⁹ and 0.4 × 10² becomes 4 × 10¹
1 kg = 10³ g, 1 g = 10³ mg, 1 km = 10³ m — convert before comparing, adding or dividing
A percentage change is done on the quantity as a whole; the answer is then written back in standard form
E on a calculator display means × 10 to the power, and never belongs on an answer line
notOnThisSpec: Engineering notation, where the power of ten is kept as a multiple of three (47 × 10³) — M7-NA-03 names standard index form, which fixes the front number between 1 and 10, and no paper read departs from it
Powers of ten that are not whole numbers, such as 10 to the power a half — the index form here is always an integer power; fractional indices are M8-NA-03

SI prefixes (nano-, micro-, mega-, giga-) offered as the answer form — every paper read prints the power of ten in full, and the metric conversions examined are the kilo-, centi-, milli- steps of M1-GM-05
Logarithms, and the use of standard form inside error bounds or upper and lower bound calculations — bounds are M3-NA-12 and M4-NA-06

mustBeAbleTo: Say what standard form is and check a number against the rule: a × 10ⁿ with the front number at least 1 and below 10
Convert an ordinary number into standard form in both directions, counting places rather than zeros, including numbers below 1 that need a negative power
Convert back from standard form to an ordinary number, including negative powers
Order a mixed list of numbers, some in standard form and some not, by putting them all into one form first and writing that conversion down
Multiply and divide in standard form without a calculator, handling the front numbers and the powers separately and re-normalising the result
Add and subtract in standard form without a calculator by making the powers equal first
Raise a standard-form number to a power, multiplying the index of ten rather than adding it
Convert units (kg and g, km and m, g and mg) before comparing, adding or dividing two quantities given in standard form
Apply a percentage increase or decrease to a standard-form quantity and return the answer to standard form
Enter standard form on a calculator with the × 10ˣ key, and turn a display such as 6.82E8 into a written answer

workedExamples.stem:
$P = 6.4 \times 10^{9}$, $Q = 2.5 \times 10^{-5}$ and $R = 4 \times 10^{3}$.
Work out the value of $\dfrac{PQ}{R}$.
Give your answer in standard form.

steps.decision: Split the job in two. Multiply the front numbers, and add the powers because $10^{9} \times 10^{-5}$ is nine tens joined to five tens taken away, leaving four. Adding a negative power is a subtraction, so the power comes down to 4 rather than up to 14.

options: Because the bigger power always wins
whyMenu.explain: The index law is the reason, and it holds whatever the signs are. Multiplying the powers instead of adding them is the commonest slip here, and it puts the answer out by many powers of ten.

steps.decision: Re-normalise straight away rather than at the end. The front number 16 is not below 10, so slide its point one place left and put that place back into the power. Doing it now keeps the next division tidy.
The same split, the other way round: divide the front numbers, subtract the powers. $1.6 \div 4 = 0.4$ needs no calculator once you see it as $16 \div 4$ with the point put back.

Re-normalise again, this time upwards: 0.4 is below 1, so the point slides one place right and the power drops by one. The value is 40 either way, but only $4 \times 10^{1}$ is in standard form, and the question asked for standard form.

options: Because the front number must be at least 1 and less than 10
Because a power of 1 is not allowed
whyMenu.explain: $0.4 \times 10^{2}$ has exactly the right value. It simply is not standard form, and the final mark on these questions is for the form.

twin.stem:
$M = 8.1 \times 10^{7}$, $N = 5 \times 10^{-3}$ and $K = 1.5 \times 10^{2}$.
Work out $\dfrac{MN}{K}$, giving your answer in standard form.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper

workedExamples.stem:
Work out $(5.4 \times 10^{-3}) + (8 \times 10^{-4})$.
Give your answer in standard form.

steps.working: $-3$ is the larger power, so aim to write both terms as something $\times 10^{-3}$.
steps.decision: Adding has no index law behind it, so the first decision is which power both numbers will share. Choosing the larger of the two keeps one number untouched and makes the other smaller, which is easier to write than a front number above 10.

options: Because addition only works when both numbers count the same thing
Because you always use the first number's power
whyMenu.explain: It is the same reason you cannot add 3 metres to 4 centimetres as they stand. The power of ten is the unit here, and both terms have to be counting in it before the front numbers can be combined.

steps.decision: Raising the power from $-4$ to $-3$ makes the power of ten ten times bigger, so the front number must become ten times smaller to keep the value the same. The point slides one place left.
Now the powers match, so add the front numbers and keep the shared power. Check the front number is still between 1 and 10 before writing it on the answer line: 6.2 is, so nothing more is needed.

twin.stem: Work out $(9.3 \times 10^{6}) - (4.5 \times 10^{5})$, giving your answer in standard form.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper

workedExamples.stem:
A photo library holds $8 \times 10^{6}$ images.
Over one year the number of images increases by 25%.
Work out the new number of images.
Give your answer in standard form.

steps.decision: The percentage is taken of the whole quantity, front number and power together. Because 25% is a quarter, only the front number needs any arithmetic: a quarter of 8 is 2, and the power of ten is untouched.

An increase means the amount found is added on. The powers already match, so the front numbers add directly. This is the step examiners report being skipped most often: the percentage gets found and then written on the answer line by itself.

options: Because an increase is the original plus the extra
Because 25% is the answer the question wants
Because the powers have to be added as well
whyMenu.explain: The question asked for the new number, not the size of the change. Reading the last line of the question again before writing the answer catches this every time.

steps.decision: The front number has reached 10, which is outside the range, so slide once more. This is the final mark: the question demanded standard form, and $10 \times 10^{6}$ is the right value written the wrong way.

twin.stem: A reservoir holds $2.5 \times 10^{5}$ cubic metres of water. After heavy rain the volume increases by 60%. Work out the new volume, giving your answer in standard form.

workedExamples.stem:
One grain of a fine sand has mass $1.1 \times 10^{-2}$ grams.
A lorry carries $7.5 \times 10^{3}$ kilograms of the sand.
Work out how many grains the lorry carries.
Give your answer in standard form, correct to 3 significant figures.

steps.decision: Before any dividing, put both masses in one unit. There are $10^{3}$ grams in a kilogram, so multiplying by $10^{3}$ raises the power by 3. Grams is the better choice here because it leaves the small number alone.

options: Because a power of ten is not a unit, so the two masses are not comparable yet
Because grams are always used in standard form
Because the lorry mass is the larger of the two
whyMenu.explain: Powers of ten only tell you the size of a number, never what it is measuring. Two quantities have to be in the same unit before any comparison or division means anything.

steps.decision: Total mass divided by the mass of one grain. A quick size check first: the total is huge and each grain is tiny, so the answer must be an enormous number, which rules out any answer with a negative power.
On Paper 2 this goes straight into the calculator using the $\times 10^{x}$ key. Some displays give $6.818181818 \times 10^{8}$ and some give 6.818181818E8; they are the same number written two ways.

Round the front number to 3 significant figures and leave the power alone, then write the power out in full. An E copied from the display onto the answer line earns nothing, because it is calculator notation rather than mathematics.

twin.stem: One droplet of an oil has mass $4.5 \times 10^{-5}$ grams. A tank holds $2.7 \times 10^{2}$ kilograms of the oil. Work out how many droplets the tank holds, giving your answer in standard form.

items.stem: Which of these is written correctly in standard form?
items.skill: Recognise the range 1 to 10 that the front number must sit in

options.feedback: The front number is between 1 and 10 and the power is a whole number, so this is the only one of the three that counts.
This has the right value, 12 400, but the front number has to be below 10. Slide the point one place left and raise the power: $1.24 \times 10^{4}$.
Again the value is right but the front number is below 1. Slide the point one place right and drop the power by one: $1.24 \times 10^{4}$.

items.stem: What is $9 \times 10^{8}$ as an ordinary number?
items.skill: Read a positive power of ten as a count of places

options.feedback: The 9 moves eight places, giving nine hundred million.
That is $9 \times 8$. The 8 is not a number to multiply by; it counts how far the digits move. Examiners saw this exact reading in Summer 2025, and every step after it is lost.
Eight zeros were written after the 9 instead of eight places moved, which lands one place short. Count places from where the point starts, just after the 9.
A positive power makes a number bigger. A negative power would have been needed for this one.

items.skill: Convert a number below 1 into standard form

options.feedback: The point slides four places right to sit after the 4, so the power is $-4$.
The sign of the power is the one thing that says whether the number is tiny or huge. $4.2 \times 10^{4}$ is 42 000.
The value is right, but 42 is not between 1 and 10. Slide one more place: $4.2 \times 10^{-4}$.
Three zeros were counted rather than four places. Count the places the point travels, not the zeros it passes.

items.skill: Multiply in standard form and re-normalise

options.feedback: $3 \times 4 = 12$ and $5 + (-2) = 3$, giving $12 \times 10^{3}$, which re-normalises to $1.2 \times 10^{4}$.
Every step was right and the value is right. The front number just has to come below 10, which costs one more slide and one more on the power.
The powers were multiplied: $5 \times (-2) = -10$. Multiplying the numbers means adding the powers, because $10^{5} \times 10^{-2}$ is five tens with two divided out.
The negative sign was dropped, so $5 + 2$ was used instead of $5 + (-2)$. A negative power pulls the answer down, not up.

items.skill: Add two numbers in standard form by matching the powers

options.feedback: $3 \times 10^{3}$ becomes $0.3 \times 10^{4}$, and $5 + 0.3 = 5.3$ at the shared power.
The fronts and the powers were both added. There is no index law for addition: $10^{4} + 10^{3}$ is not $10^{7}$, it is 11 000.
The fronts were added as though the powers already matched. Rewrite one number first so that both read $\times 10^{4}$, then add.
The front numbers were matched to $10^{4}$ but the smaller power was carried down to the answer. Whichever power you convert to is the power the answer keeps.

items.stem: Which of these is the largest?
items.skill: Order numbers in standard form by comparing powers first

options.feedback: $-2$ is the highest power of the three, so this is the largest at 0.02, even though 2 is the smallest front number.
The 9 catches the eye, but the power decides first. $9 \times 10^{-4}$ is 0.0009, well under 0.02.
This is 0.006, which sits between the other two. Compare the powers, and only look at the front numbers when the powers tie.

items.stem: Sample $A$ has mass $3.4 \times 10^{5}$ grams. Sample $B$ has mass $4 \times 10^{2}$ kilograms. Which is heavier?
items.skill: Match the units before comparing two quantities in standard form

options.text: $B$, because it is 400 kg against 340 kg
options.feedback: Both masses in one unit, then compared. That single conversion line is what the scheme is looking for.
The powers are measuring different things, so they cannot be compared as they stand. In kilograms, $A$ is $3.4 \times 10^{2}$, and 340 is less than 400.

options.text: $A$, because 3.4 is nearly as big as 4 and its power is much bigger
options.feedback: Convert before you reason about size at all. Examiners in Summer 2024 reported a whole group comparing the printed numbers without converting.

items.stem: A calculator display reads 3.6E-05. The question asks for standard form. What goes on the answer line?
items.skill: Turn a calculator display into standard form on the answer line

options.feedback: The E is the calculator's shorthand for times ten to the power. Written out in full, it earns the mark.
The display has been copied rather than read. E is not mathematical notation, so it earns nothing on an answer line.
This is the right value as an ordinary number, but the question asked for standard form, and the last mark on these questions is for the form.
This is a different number altogether, about 0.0017. The power belongs to the ten, never to the front number.

parts.stem: Write $2\,970\,000$ in standard form.

accept: 2.97 x 10^6 written with any multiplication sign

hints: Where does the decimal point sit at the moment? Just after the last zero.
Slide it left until only one digit is in front of it, counting the places.
Six places, so the power is 6.
parts.workedSolution: The point starts after the final zero. Sliding it left to sit between the 2 and the 9 takes six places, so $2\,970\,000 = 2.97 \times 10^{6}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The value is right but the front number must come below 10. One more slide left gives $2.97 \times 10^{6}$.

parts.stem: Write $0.000\,405$ in standard form.
hints: The number is below 1, so the power will be negative.
Slide the point right until it sits just after the 4.
Count places, not zeros: there are three zeros but four places.
parts.workedSolution: Sliding the point right to sit after the 4 takes four places, and sliding right means a negative power, so $0.000\,405 = 4.05 \times 10^{-4}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right but the sign of the power is not. A number below 1 always needs a negative power; $4.05 \times 10^{4}$ is 40 500.
Three zeros were counted instead of four places. The point has to travel past the zeros and past the 4 itself, which is one more place than the zeros suggest.

parts.stem: Write $5.06 \times 10^{-4}$ as an ordinary number.
hints: A negative power slides the point left.
Four places left from just after the 5.
Keep the zero that sits inside the number as well as the ones in front.
parts.workedSolution: Sliding the point four places left from after the 5 gives $0.000\,506$. The zero between the 5 and the 6 stays where it is; it is part of the digits, not part of the sliding.

commonErrors.feedback: A negative power makes a number smaller, so the answer is below 1. The minus sign is doing the same job as a division by $10^{4}$.

parts.stem: Write $84 \times 10^{5}$ in standard form.
hints: This is already a number times a power of ten, but it is not standard form yet.
84 has to come below 10.
Sliding the point one place left costs one on the power, so the power goes up by one.

commonErrors.feedback: The power was moved the wrong way. Making the front number smaller must make the power bigger, or the value changes.

parts.stem:
Work out $(3 \times 10^{5}) \times (2.5 \times 10^{-8})$.
Give your answer in standard form.
hints: Front numbers together, powers together.
Multiplying means adding the powers, and one of them is negative.
parts.workedSolution: $3 \times 2.5 = 7.5$ and $10^{5} \times 10^{-8} = 10^{5 + (-8)} = 10^{-3}$, so the answer is $7.5 \times 10^{-3}$. The front number is already between 1 and 10, so nothing more is needed.

commonErrors.feedback: The powers were multiplied rather than added: $5 \times (-8) = -40$. Multiplying two powers of ten adds their indices, which is the index law $10^{a} \times 10^{b} = 10^{a+b}$.
The minus sign was lost when the powers were added. $5 + (-8)$ is a subtraction, so the power finishes below zero, and the answer is a small number.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper

parts.stem:
Work out $(7.2 \times 10^{6}) \div (9 \times 10^{-2})$.
Give your answer in standard form.
hints: Divide the front numbers, subtract the powers.
Subtracting a negative power adds: $6 - (-2) = 8$.
0.8 is below 1, so the answer needs one more slide before it is in standard form.
parts.workedSolution: $7.2 \div 9 = 0.8$ and $10^{6} \div 10^{-2} = 10^{6 - (-2)} = 10^{8}$, giving $0.8 \times 10^{8}$. Since 0.8 is below 1, slide the point one place right and drop the power by one: $8 \times 10^{7}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The division was done correctly, which is the first mark. The answer mark needs the front number between 1 and 10: slide right once and take one off the power to get $8 \times 10^{7}$.
The powers were subtracted as $6 - 2$. Taking away a negative power adds it on, so the power is 8 before re-normalising, not 4.

parts.stem:
Work out $(6 \times 10^{-4}) + (3.5 \times 10^{-3})$.
Give your answer in standard form.

scheme.for: both terms written at one power, e.g. $0.6 \times 10^{-3} + 3.5 \times 10^{-3}$, or both written as ordinary numbers

hints: There is no index law for addition, so the powers have to match first.
Rewrite $6 \times 10^{-4}$ at the power $-3$.
Raising the power by one slides that front number's point one place left: $0.6 \times 10^{-3}$.
parts.workedSolution: $6 \times 10^{-4} = 0.6 \times 10^{-3}$, so the sum is $0.6 \times 10^{-3} + 3.5 \times 10^{-3} = 4.1 \times 10^{-3}$. As ordinary numbers this is $0.0006 + 0.0035 = 0.0041$, which is the same thing.

commonErrors.feedback: The front numbers and the powers were both added. Addition has no index law: two numbers can only be added once they are counting in the same power of ten.
The fronts were added as though the powers already matched. Convert one term first, then add: $0.6 + 3.5 = 4.1$ at the power $-3$.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper

parts.stem:
Work out $(5.2 \times 10^{9}) - (7 \times 10^{8})$.
Give your answer in standard form.

scheme.for: both terms written at one power, e.g. $5.2 \times 10^{9} - 0.7 \times 10^{9}$

hints: Match the powers before subtracting.
Write $7 \times 10^{8}$ at the power 9.
parts.workedSolution: $7 \times 10^{8} = 0.7 \times 10^{9}$, so the subtraction is $5.2 \times 10^{9} - 0.7 \times 10^{9} = 4.5 \times 10^{9}$. The front number is between 1 and 10, so that is the answer.

commonErrors.feedback: The front numbers were matched correctly but the answer kept the smaller power. Once $7 \times 10^{8}$ has been rewritten as $0.7 \times 10^{9}$, the shared power 9 is the power the answer carries.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper

parts.stem:
Work out $(2 \times 10^{5})^{3}$.
Give your answer in standard form.
hints: The cube applies to everything inside the bracket.
Cube the front number, and multiply the power by 3.
parts.workedSolution: $(2 \times 10^{5})^{3} = 2^{3} \times (10^{5})^{3} = 8 \times 10^{15}$. The power inside a bracket is multiplied by the outside power, not added to itself.

commonErrors.feedback: The bracket was treated as a multiplication by 3, giving $2 \times 3$ and $5 + 3$. A cube means three copies multiplied together, so the front number is cubed and the power is tripled.
The front number was cubed but the power was left alone. Everything inside the bracket is cubed, the power of ten included.

parts.stem:
$A = 4.2 \times 10^{-3}$
$B = 0.000\,52$
$C = 3.9 \times 10^{-4}$
List $A$, $B$ and $C$ from smallest to largest.
You must show your working.

options.feedback: As ordinary numbers, 0.000 39, 0.000 52 and 0.0042. The conversions are two of the three marks, so write them down even when the order is obvious to you.
The front numbers 3.9, 4.2 and 5.2 were compared. $A$ has a power of $-3$ against the other two at $-4$, so $A$ is about ten times bigger than either of them.
This is the right order reversed. The question asked you to start with the smallest, and the answer boxes are filled left to right.

scheme.for: all three written in one common form, either as ordinary numbers or all at the same power of ten

hints: Put all three into the same form before comparing anything.
Ordinary numbers are easiest here because one of them is already written that way.
$B$ is $5.2 \times 10^{-4}$, so $B$ and $C$ share a power and the front numbers decide between them.
parts.workedSolution: As ordinary numbers, $A = 0.0042$, $B = 0.000\,52$ and $C = 0.000\,39$. Comparing them gives $C < B < A$, so the order is $C$, $B$, $A$. In standard form the same working reads $C = 3.9 \times 10^{-4}$, $B = 5.2 \times 10^{-4}$, $A = 42 \times 10^{-4}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The order is right, but two of the three marks are for the conversions. Writing every number in one form, even briefly, is what the scheme is paid to see.
The front numbers were compared before the powers. $A$ has the largest power of the three, which makes it the largest number whatever its front number looks like.

parts.stem:
Sample $X$ has mass $6.4 \times 10^{5}$ milligrams.
Sample $Y$ has mass $5.9 \times 10^{2}$ grams.
Work out which sample is heavier.
You must show your working.

options.text: $X$, because it is 640 g against 590 g
options.feedback: Both masses put into grams first, then compared. That conversion line carries the method mark.

options.text: $Y$, because $5.9 \times 10^{2}$ grams is the larger unit
options.feedback: The unit being larger does not make the quantity larger. In grams, $X$ is $6.4 \times 10^{2}$, which is 640 against $Y$'s 590.

options.text: $X$, because $10^{5}$ is a bigger power than $10^{2}$
options.feedback: The choice happens to be right, but the reason is not, and the marks here are for the conversion. Powers attached to different units are not comparable.

scheme.for: both masses written in one unit, e.g. $6.4 \times 10^{5}\text{ mg} = 6.4 \times 10^{2}\text{ g}$, or $5.9 \times 10^{2}\text{ g} = 5.9 \times 10^{5}\text{ mg}$
$X$ chosen, with the two converted masses seen

hints: One label is in milligrams and one is in grams, so nothing can be compared yet.
There are $10^{3}$ milligrams in a gram.
Dividing by $10^{3}$ takes 3 off the power: $6.4 \times 10^{5}\text{ mg} = 6.4 \times 10^{2}\text{ g}$.
parts.workedSolution: There are 1000 milligrams in a gram, so $X = 6.4 \times 10^{5}\text{ mg} = 6.4 \times 10^{2}\text{ g} = 640\text{ g}$. Sample $Y$ is $5.9 \times 10^{2}\text{ g} = 590\text{ g}$. Since $640 > 590$, sample $X$ is heavier.

commonErrors.feedback: The two powers are attached to different units, so comparing them compares nothing. Summer 2024 examiners reported a sizeable group doing exactly this. Convert first, then compare.

parts.stem:
A plantation contains $6 \times 10^{5}$ trees.
Over ten years the number of trees increases by 70%.
Work out the new number of trees.
Give your answer in standard form.
hints: Take the percentage of the whole quantity: front number and power together.
10% is $6 \times 10^{4}$, so 70% is seven of those.
After adding, check whether the front number is still below 10.
parts.workedSolution: 70% of $6 \times 10^{5}$ is $0.7 \times 6 \times 10^{5} = 4.2 \times 10^{5}$. Adding it on gives $6 \times 10^{5} + 4.2 \times 10^{5} = 10.2 \times 10^{5}$. The front number 10.2 is not below 10, so slide once more: $1.02 \times 10^{6}$. The multiplier route reaches the same place: $1.7 \times 6 \times 10^{5} = 10.2 \times 10^{5}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the size of the increase, which earns the first mark. The question asked for the new number, so it still has to be added to the original.
The arithmetic is complete and both of the first two marks are safe. The last mark is for the form: 10.2 is not below 10, so one more slide gives $1.02 \times 10^{6}$.

parts.stem:
Calculate $(4.7 \times 10^{8}) \times (6.3 \times 10^{-3})$.
Give your answer in standard form, correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Use the $\times 10^{x}$ key rather than typing the digits and a power.
Round the front number only; the power is not part of the significant figures.
$2.961 \rightarrow 2.96$ to 3 significant figures.
parts.workedSolution: $4.7 \times 6.3 = 29.61$ and $8 + (-3) = 5$, giving $29.61 \times 10^{5} = 2.961 \times 10^{6}$. To 3 significant figures that is $2.96 \times 10^{6}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the display rather than the answer. E means times ten to the power, so write it out: $2.96 \times 10^{6}$.
The multiplication is right, so the method mark is safe. The front number must come below 10, which moves the power from 5 up to 6.

parts.stem:
In standard form,
$(4 \times 10^{p}) \times (2 \times 10^{q}) = 8 \times 10^{9}$
$(4 \times 10^{p}) \div (2 \times 10^{q}) = 2 \times 10^{3}$
Find the value of $p$.
hints: The front numbers already work: $4 \times 2 = 8$ and $4 \div 2 = 2$, so they tell you nothing about $p$ and $q$.
Multiplying adds the powers, so $p + q = 9$. Dividing subtracts them, so $p - q = 3$.
Add the two equations to remove $q$.
parts.workedSolution: Multiplying adds the powers, so $p + q = 9$; dividing subtracts them, so $p - q = 3$. Adding the two equations gives $2p = 12$, so $p = 6$.

commonErrors.feedback: The powers were treated as being multiplied, giving $pq = 9$. Multiplying two powers of ten adds their indices; it is the front numbers that get multiplied.

parts.stem: Find the value of $q$.
hints: Put your value of $p$ back into either equation.
parts.workedSolution: Substituting $p = 6$ into $p + q = 9$ gives $q = 3$. Checking both lines: $(4 \times 10^{6}) \times (2 \times 10^{3}) = 8 \times 10^{9}$ and $(4 \times 10^{6}) \div (2 \times 10^{3}) = 2 \times 10^{3}$.

questions.solutionProgram: p + q = 9; p - q = 3; 2p = 12 so p = 6, q = 3; check 4e6*2e3 = 8e9 and 4e6/2e3 = 2e3

parts.stem:
$A = (6 \times 10^{-4}) + (3 \times 10^{2})$
$B = (6 \times 10^{-4}) \times (3 \times 10^{2})$
$C = (6 \times 10^{-4}) \div (3 \times 10^{2})$
List $A$, $B$ and $C$ from smallest to largest.
You must show your working.

options.feedback: $C = 2 \times 10^{-6}$, $B = 1.8 \times 10^{-1}$ and $A$ is a fraction over 300. Two of the three marks are for those values appearing on the page.
$B$ and $C$ were separated by their front numbers, 1.8 against 2. Their powers are $-1$ and $-6$, so $C$ is the smaller by a factor of about a hundred thousand.
$A$ has been undervalued, which usually means the addition was done by combining the powers. Adding $6 \times 10^{-4}$ to $3 \times 10^{2}$ barely changes it, so $A$ stays just above 300.
This is the right order reversed. The question asked you to start with the smallest.

scheme.for: a correct method for at least two of the three, e.g. powers added for $B$ and subtracted for $C$

hints: Work out all three before ordering anything.
Only the addition needs the powers matched; the other two are front numbers and powers handled separately.
$B = 18 \times 10^{-2}$, which re-normalises to $1.8 \times 10^{-1}$.
parts.workedSolution:
$A$: the powers must match, so $6 \times 10^{-4} = 0.000\,000\,6 \times 10^{2}$ and $A = 300.0006$, which is a little over 300.
$B$: $6 \times 3 = 18$ and $-4 + 2 = -2$, so $B = 18 \times 10^{-2} = 1.8 \times 10^{-1} = 0.18$.
$C$: $6 \div 3 = 2$ and $-4 - 2 = -6$, so $C = 2 \times 10^{-6} = 0.000\,002$.
Smallest first: $C$, $B$, $A$.

commonErrors.feedback: $A$ was treated as though addition had an index law, giving $6 + 3 = 9$ and $-4 + 2 = -2$. Only multiplication adds the powers; addition needs them matched first.
The order is right and no marks follow it, because the paper said to show your working. Write the three values down, however roughly, and two more marks are there.
$B$ and $C$ were ordered by their front numbers, 1.8 against 2. Their powers are $-1$ and $-6$, so $C$ is the smaller of the two by a factor of about a hundred thousand.

context.setting: The mass of ice on a glacier, measured in tonnes

parts.stem:
A glacier held $1.6 \times 10^{9}$ tonnes of ice.
Over twenty years the mass of ice decreased by 35%.
Work out the new mass of ice.
Give your answer in standard form.

scheme.for: 35% of $1.6 \times 10^{9}$ found, i.e. $5.6 \times 10^{8}$ or $560\,000\,000$; or the multiplier 0.65 seen
subtracted: $1.04 \times 10^{9}$ or $1\,040\,000\,000$ reached in any form

hints: A decrease means the amount found is taken away from the original.
Or go straight there with the multiplier $1 - 0.35 = 0.65$.
parts.workedSolution: 35% of $1.6 \times 10^{9}$ is $0.35 \times 1.6 \times 10^{9} = 0.56 \times 10^{9} = 5.6 \times 10^{8}$. Taking it away gives $1.6 \times 10^{9} - 0.56 \times 10^{9} = 1.04 \times 10^{9}$ tonnes. The multiplier route is quicker: $0.65 \times 1.6 = 1.04$, so the answer is $1.04 \times 10^{9}$ tonnes, and the front number is already in range.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass of ice lost, which earns the first mark. The question asked for the mass remaining, so it has to come off the original.
The change was added rather than taken away. Read the verb once more before the last line: decreased means the answer has to be smaller than the number you started with.
$1.6 \times 10^{9}$ was read as $1.6 \times 9$. The 9 counts places, not a quantity to multiply by, and a glacier measured in single tonnes should have felt wrong.

context.setting: The mass of a single bacterium and the mass of a colony

parts.stem:
A colony of bacteria has mass $3.8 \times 10^{-4}$ kilograms.
Write this mass in grams.
Give your answer in standard form.
hints: There are $10^{3}$ grams in a kilogram.
Multiplying by $10^{3}$ raises the power by 3.
parts.workedSolution: Multiplying by 1000 to change kilograms into grams raises the power by 3: $3.8 \times 10^{-4}\text{ kg} = 3.8 \times 10^{-1}\text{ g}$, which is 0.38 g.

commonErrors.feedback: The power was lowered by 3 instead of raised. Grams are smaller than kilograms, so the same mass needs a bigger number of them.

parts.stem:
One bacterium has mass $9.5 \times 10^{-13}$ grams.
Work out how many bacteria are in the colony.
Give your answer in standard form.

scheme.for: $\dfrac{3.8 \times 10^{-1}}{9.5 \times 10^{-13}}$ seen, with both masses in grams

hints: Divide the mass of the colony by the mass of one bacterium.
Both masses must be in the same unit first, which is what part (a) gave you.

commonErrors.feedback: The colony mass was used in kilograms while the bacterium was in grams, so the answer is a thousand times too small. Part (a) exists to prevent exactly this.
The division is right, so the method mark is safe. The front number has to reach at least 1: slide right once and drop the power to get $4 \times 10^{11}$.

parts.stem: Write your answer to part (b) as an ordinary number.
hints: A power of 11 slides the point eleven places right.
Start from 4 and count the places, not the zeros you write.
Four hundred thousand million.
parts.workedSolution: $4 \times 10^{11}$ moves the 4 eleven places, giving $400\,000\,000\,000$.

commonErrors.feedback: $4 \times 10^{11}$ was read as $4 \times 11$. The power counts the places the digits move; it is never a number to multiply the front number by.

parts.stem:
Work out $(4 \times 10^{5})^{2}$.
Give your answer in standard form.
hints: Square everything inside the bracket.
Squaring a power of ten doubles it.
16 is not below 10, so one more slide is needed.
parts.workedSolution: $(4 \times 10^{5})^{2} = 4^{2} \times 10^{5 \times 2} = 16 \times 10^{10}$, and re-normalising gives $1.6 \times 10^{11}$.

commonErrors.feedback: Both squarings are right, so the method mark is yours. The answer mark is for the form: 16 becomes 1.6 and the power rises from 10 to 11.
The power was added to itself as $5 + 2$ instead of multiplied by 2. A square is the bracket times itself, so $10^{5} \times 10^{5} = 10^{10}$.

parts.stem:
Work out $(1.5 \times 10^{-2}) + (9 \times 10^{-3})$.
Give your answer in standard form.

scheme.for: both terms at one power, e.g. $1.5 \times 10^{-2} + 0.9 \times 10^{-2}$, or $0.015 + 0.009$

hints: Match the powers before adding anything.
Write $9 \times 10^{-3}$ at the power $-2$.

commonErrors.feedback: Both halves were added, giving $1.5 + 9 = 10.5$ and $-2 + (-3) = -5$. Addition has no index law; the powers have to be made equal instead.
The front numbers were added without matching the powers first, so 9 was counted as nine hundredths rather than nine thousandths. Convert, then add.

findTheMistake.stem: Erin was asked: a data centre stores $7 \times 10^{6}$ files. The number of files increases by 20%. Work out the new number of files, giving your answer in standard form. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The first line reads $10^{6}$ as a 6 to multiply by. The 6 is a count of places, so $7 \times 10^{6}$ is seven million, not 42. Every line after it is competent percentage work applied to a number about a hundred and seventy thousand times too small, so none of it can be credited.
findTheMistake.feedback: The percentage method was sound, and on the right number it would have scored everything. Examiners in Summer 2025 reported this exact reading on a question about a reservoir. One habit fixes it: before calculating, say the number out loud as an ordinary number. Seven million files is believable for a data centre; 42 files is not.

findTheMistake.stem: Daniel was asked to work out $(4 \times 10^{5}) + (3 \times 10^{4})$ without a calculator, giving his answer in standard form. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 uses the multiplication rule on an addition. Adding the powers is what you do when the two numbers are multiplied together; here they are being added, and there is no index law for that. The powers have to be made equal first, and then only the front numbers move.
findTheMistake.feedback: Line 1 is the right instinct in the wrong place: the front numbers do add, but only once both terms are counting in the same power of ten. Examiners in November 2025 named addition as the hardest of these operations without a calculator. A size check catches it too, since $7 \times 10^{9}$ is more than ten thousand times the largest number in the question.

findTheMistake.stem: Orla was asked which is heavier: parcel $P$ at $2.6 \times 10^{6}$ milligrams, or parcel $Q$ at $3 \times 10^{3}$ grams. She had to show her working. Her working:
studentWorking: P has power 6, Q has power 3
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 compares two powers that are attached to different units, so they are not measuring the same thing. A power of ten records size, never what is being measured. In grams, $P$ is $2.6 \times 10^{3}$, which is 2600 g against $Q$'s 3000 g, so the conclusion is the other way round.
findTheMistake.feedback: Comparing the powers is the right move once the units agree, and it is a quick way to sort standard-form numbers. Summer 2024 examiners reported over half the M8 entry converting one quantity and comparing as though both were done, with others not converting at all. Make the conversion line the first thing on the page whenever two units appear.

prompts.prompt: What does it mean for a number to be written in standard form?
prompts.answer: It is written as $a \times 10^{n}$ where $a$ is at least 1 and less than 10, and $n$ is a whole number, positive or negative.
keyWords: a times ten to the n

prompts.prompt: How do you convert an ordinary number into standard form?
prompts.answer: Slide the decimal point until exactly one non-zero digit is in front of it, and count the places. Sliding left gives a positive power, sliding right gives a negative one. Count places, not zeros.

prompts.prompt: How do you multiply or divide two numbers in standard form?
prompts.answer: Handle the front numbers and the powers separately: multiply or divide the front numbers, add the powers when multiplying and subtract them when dividing. Then re-normalise so the front number is between 1 and 10.

prompts.prompt: How do you add or subtract two numbers in standard form without a calculator?
prompts.answer: Rewrite one of them so that both have the same power of ten, usually the larger one. Then add or subtract the front numbers, keep the shared power, and re-normalise if the front number has left the range.

prompts.prompt: A question increases a standard-form quantity by a percentage. What are the three things the marks are for?
prompts.answer: Finding the percentage of the whole quantity, adding it on to the original, and writing the final answer back in standard form with the front number between 1 and 10.

prompts.prompt: Two quantities are given in standard form but in different units. What is the first line you write?
prompts.answer: The conversion of one of them into the other's unit. A power of ten is not a unit, so the powers cannot be compared until both quantities are measuring in the same thing.

prompts.prompt: Your working has reached $0.4 \times 10^{7}$. What do you do, and why?
prompts.answer: Re-normalise to $4 \times 10^{6}$. The value is right but the front number must be at least 1 and below 10, and the final mark on these questions is for the form rather than the size.
Raise both parts to the power: $a^{k} \times 10^{nk}$. The power of ten is multiplied by $k$, not added to itself in the front number. Then re-normalise.

prompts.prompt: Your calculator display reads 5.3E-04. What do you write on the answer line?
prompts.answer: $5.3 \times 10^{-4}$. The E is the calculator's shorthand for times ten to the power, and it earns nothing if it is copied onto an answer line.

prompts.prompt: An ordering question says to show your working. What has to appear on the page?
prompts.answer: Every number converted to one common form, either all as ordinary numbers or all at the same power of ten. The order on its own scores nothing, however it was found.

findings.asked: Compare two masses in standard form given in different units.
findings.wentWrong: 1.05 x 10 to the 7 was treated as 1.05 x 7; many never converted grams and kilograms to one unit.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Converted both to kilograms (10500 kg and 15000 kg) and compared.

findings.asked: Convert and compare weights in standard form and different units.
findings.wentWrong: Over half converted one weight and compared; a sizeable minority ignored the units and compared the bare numbers.
findings.rule: Standard form does not remove the need to match units.

findings.asked: Write 463 in standard form; a calculation with a power of -1.
findings.wentWrong: A fifth could not write 463 in standard form; only a third handled the negative power.
findings.rule: 10 to the minus 1 means divide by 10.

findings.asked: Increase a standard-form number by 30% and give the answer in standard form.
findings.wentWrong: Some found 30% but did not add it; others miscalculated 30%; a common slip left 1 170 000 000 as an ordinary number; a few wrote 9 x 10 to the 8 as 9 x 8.
findings.rule: Add the increase, then rewrite as a x 10 to the n with 1 <= a < 10.

findings.asked: Standard form combined with a percentage increase.
findings.wentWrong: Over a third scored nothing; nearly 40% got all three marks.
findings.rule: Do the percentage on the ordinary number, then convert back.

findings.asked: Standard-form calculations without a calculator, including an addition.
findings.wentWrong: Thirty per cent could not manipulate them; the addition was hardest; a fifth got full marks.
findings.rule: To add, write both with the same power of ten first.

findings.asked: Order three numbers given in different forms, showing working.
findings.wentWrong: Working was required; guesses scored nothing; converting to ordinary numbers or to matching standard form both worked, but few managed all three.
findings.rule: Show the conversion for every number.
